"If states were free to attack one another based on their own assessments of possible future threats, what would be left of the international legal order?" Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi has asked in an opinion piece for Japan's Kyodo News.
"This question," Araghchi wrote, "goes well beyond the political dispute between Iran and the United States."
"It concerns one of the fundamental principles on which the international order established after the Second World War rests: the use of force is governed by law, and no state, however powerful, is entitled to place its own judgment above binding rules of international law," the article read.
He said the US-Israeli strikes constituted a clear violation of the prohibition on the use of force and an infringement of Iran's sovereignty.
"Their legality must be assessed against the U.N. Charter and established principles of international law, not against political arguments or justifications advanced after military operations have begun," he wrote.
He said the US had neither obtained UN Security Council authorisation nor established grounds for invoking self-defence under Article 51, which permits force in response to an armed attack.
The attacks on schools, sports stadiums, civilian infrastructure, and Iranian nuclear facilities subject to International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards raise further questions under international law, and they must be examined under international humanitarian law.

The administration would extend the waiver of the more than 100-year-old Jones Act, Reuters reported, citing industry sources.

In Jaba’, south of Jenin, Israeli forces stormed the town, firing live ammunition and tear gas, and shot a young Palestinian man in the thigh, the Palestinian Red Crescent Society said.

The United Arab Emirates remains the key trading hub for smuggled gold and conflict gold, a new report from Switzerland’s Swissaid foundation has found.
Despite the introduction in 2023 of legislation intended to curb illegal flows, the UAE, which is now the world’s second largest gold trading hub after Switzerland, imported at least 591 tonnes of illicit gold into the country in 2024.
Illicit gold refers to that which was either smuggled to the UAE - most often to the gold markets of Dubai, the second largest Emirate - without being able to be traced, or that comes from countries at war, including Yemen, Sudan and Russia.
The UAE remains by far the main destination for gold linked to armed conflicts in Africa, according to Swissaid. It also continues to be a major destination for gold exports from countries subject to international sanctions.
“The findings of this study are deeply concerning. They show that the United Arab Emirates remains a hub for smuggled and conflict gold,” said Marc Ummel, head of Swissaid’s commodities unit and co-author of the study.
In 2024, the UAE imported at least 174.5 tonnes of gold from Russia (directly and indirectly via Armenia), Yemen and Sudan (directly and indirectly), Swissaid found. The entire volume from these three countries can, the organisation said, “be considered as conflict gold”.

A senior Chabad rabbi has been criticised by his own movement after he said it was permissible to kill Jewish Israeli politicians who worked with Arabs.
Gedalia Axelrod, a senior cleric in the Chabad-Lubavitch Hasidic movement, issued a halakhic ruling earlier this week in which he said that Jewish politicians who form a government backed by Palestinian citizens of Israel were "din rodef", which roughly translates as "law of the pursuer".
Under Jewish religious law, a rodef is someone who poses a threat to another person's life and may be stopped by any means necessary.
The doctrine was previously invoked by Yitzhak Rabin’s assassin, Yigal Amir, to justify the prime minister’s killing in 1995.
Axelrod wrote that collaboration with Arab parties "poses a terrible danger to the people of Israel in the Holy Land and around the world".
Collaboration could either take the form of inviting Arab parties to join a governing coalition, or even relying on their support from outside it.
Swift condemnation
Axelrod's comments were swiftly condemned by the leadership of his religious movement, with Chabad spokesperson Rabbi Shimi Segal clarifying that his statements did not represent the official Chabad position.
“Chabad’s official halachic positions are determined exclusively by the Chabad Rabbinical Court, in accordance with the Rebbe’s instructions,” he said.

It was half past five in the afternoon when Bahij Abdallah saw a white object pass overhead.
He was outside a pumping station in Ebel el-Saqi, in the hills above Marjayoun, checking on an open water reservoir. He had sat down on a stone step with his phone in his hand, while three colleagues remained inside.
At first, he thought the white thing was a drone.
“Suddenly, it stopped in the air for a second, turned, and fell on the station,” Abdallah told Middle East Eye. “Then the smoke and the fire started.”
The phone flew out of his hand. He felt a wall of air, and then metal pushing into his body. He looked down and saw blood dripping from his face. His shoulder was burning. When he stood up, he saw that his shoe had been cut open.
Abdallah, an electrical maintenance employee with the South Lebanon Water Establishment (SLWE), the state utility that supplies drinking water to two governorates, had been doing what he does most days: running the station and monitoring it.
The facility is well known in the region and clearly marked, he said. “There are signs, and vehicles with the name and logo on them, that it belongs to the South Lebanon Water Establishment, which is a government body. And we were wearing the work uniform.”
The attack occurred on 9 June 2026, five days after Israel and the Lebanese government announced in Washington that they had agreed to a ceasefire.

Pro-Palestinian activists have asked a French court to ban an Israeli real estate fair in Paris marketing Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem, AFP reported on Thursday.
The Franco-Palestinian NIDAL association filed an emergency motion with a court against the 9th Icube real estate and investment salon, arguing that the fair violates human rights.
The event is scheduled for Sunday at the European Centre for Judaism in the French capital. Other major cities have seen similar uproars over Israeli real estate fairs.
NIDAL asked the court to either order the head of the Paris police force to ban the event outright or to ensure that the event does not sell property in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, whose occupation by Israel since 1967 is considered illegal under international law.
Before taking legal action, the group said they had sent a letter to the Paris police on 5 November, which went unanswered.
In the filing, seen by AFP, the rights group says that marketing Israeli settlements in the occupied territories contributes to the forced displacement of the Palestinian people through population transfer - a practice prohibited by international law and classified as a war crime under the French penal code.
In particular, the activists highlighted that BH Nadlan, a company that markets settlements in both East Jerusalem and the West Bank on its website, will be present at the fair.
They also pointed to the fair's official guide's offer of a "significant" financial "bonus" for newcomers settling in "Judea and Samaria", the Israeli term for the occupied West Bank.

Saudi Arabia is feeling the pinch of a liquidity crisis as bank deposits slow and the economy comes under pressure from the US-Israeli war on Iran, a new report from Bank of America says.
In a note to clients, Bank of America said Saudi Arabia is grappling with “contagion” caused by liquidity tightness in the UAE and a rapid slowdown in the kingdom’s own economy, according to an article published on Bloomberg on Tuesday.
The report said Saudi banks are feeling the pain in the UAE, which is also grappling with fallout from the Iran war and tighter liquidity. Saudi banks are closely linked to their Emirati neighbours, with a high number of interbank transactions contributing to deposits at Saudi banks.
At the same time, the Saudi economy is under strain and government entities are making withdrawals from Saudi banks. But loan demand is high, which is effectively raising the cost of Saudi money.
The liquidity strain is notable for Saudi Arabia because its currency is directly pegged to the US dollar, along with Gulf states including the UAE, Qatar, Oman, and Bahrain.

UN humanitarian chief says 'no more excuses' on opening Gaza crossing
UN under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator Tom Fletcher said on Wednesday that there cannot be any more delays in opening the border crossings into Gaza to deliver humanitarian aid.
"No more delays. No more excuses. We must open all the crossings, mobilize the whole humanitarian community, and get our full Winter plan delivered for Gaza," Fletcher wrote in a post on X.
He said that certain countries supporting aid deliveries to Gaza told him that delivering winter supplies will have to wait for the formation of an Israeli government.
“This is not an acceptable excuse,” he added, citing international law and the consequences of delays, blockages and funding cuts.

Saudi-led coalition says two Houthi ballistic missiles destroyed, explosions heard in Aden
The Saudi-led coalition said on Wednesday that its air defences intercepted and destroyed two ballistic missiles launched by the Houthis towards Saudi Arabia’s western region.
This comes after an earlier statement from the coalition, which said the Houthis targeted Mecca and the southern region of Saudi Arabia - accusations which the group has denied.
Meanwhile, Al Jazeera reported that two explosions have been heard in the southern Yemeni city of Aden.
